title: Planning a MAIC from the estimator's influence function, not from n or Kish ESS
question: Before any data exist, which planning quantity predicts the precision a MAIC will achieve: nominal sample size, Kish effective sample size, or the estimator's influence-function variance evaluated at posited source and target laws?
answer: The influence-function variance. It predicted the achieved SD within 10% in 85% of 72 scenarios, missing only at 150 patients with 10% prevalence. Kish ESS was within 10% in 58% and understated the achieved SD in 99% of scenarios, so it is optimistic, not the conservative quantity it is usually taken to be; nominal n was within 10% in 21%.
findings: Planned SE over achieved SD, median (range): influence function 0.963 (0.827 to 1.023); Kish ESS 0.912 (0.745 to 1.004); nominal n 0.797 (0.541 to 0.985).
Kish ESS understated the achieved SD in 99% of scenarios; its error grew with the target shift.
All 11 influence-function misses were at 150 patients and 10% prevalence; its median ratio was 0.908 at 150 patients and 0.981 at 1000.
The refuting sentence, that nominal n with an overlap adjustment is good enough, fails its registered criterion (58% of scenarios within 10% against the 90% required).
not_answered: The planner is assumed to know the source and target laws. Binary outcome, anchored-side precision and MAIC on means only; the unanchored bias floor and survival outcomes are not run. Peer review has not been done.
design: Binary-outcome MAIC with 2 or 5 covariates, 72 scenarios crossing total size (150, 400, 1000), target shift, dimension, allocation and prevalence; three planned SEs computed from the posited laws compared with the SD achieved over replicates.
estimand: SD of the MAIC estimate of the target marginal log odds ratio
